01.actor: The orphaned heirs of a man who willed a palm tree to his daughter
01.event: The heirs divided the estate and gave the daughter no palm tree, and Rav Yosef first thought this was like the mishna's case.
01.turn: Abaye objected that the cases differ, since here the tree is held by all the heirs.
01.outcome: Abaye ruled the heirs must give her a palm tree and redivide the estate.
01.summary: A man told his heirs to give his daughter a palm tree. The heirs split the estate and gave her none. Rav Yosef thought she had no claim, as in the mishna, but Abaye said the cases differ because the tree belongs to all of them. They had to give her a tree and divide the estate again.

02.actor: A man who deposited silk with Rav Dimi
02.event: The man left silk with Rav Dimi, who died without saying anything, and the claimant went to Rabbi Abba.
02.turn: Rabbi Abba reasoned that Rav Dimi was not wealthy and that the claimant had described the silk.
02.outcome: Rabbi Abba awarded the silk to the claimant.
02.summary: A man left silk at Rav Dimi's house, and Rav Dimi died without saying whose it was. The man came before Rabbi Abba. Rabbi Abba knew Rav Dimi was not rich and the man gave a distinguishing mark of the silk, so he ruled the silk was the man's.

03.missing: This is a legal debate: Rav Hillel cites a written list against Ameimar's ruling and Rav Ashi answers. No event is narrated.

04.actor: A man who recalled being immersed as a child to eat teruma
04.event: He casually said he remembered being taken out of school and immersed so he could eat teruma, and that his friends called him Yohanan who eats hallot.
04.turn: His offhand remark was taken as reliable evidence of priestly status.
04.outcome: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi elevated him to the priesthood on his word.
04.summary: A man mentioned in passing that, as a child, he was taken from school and immersed so he could eat teruma that evening. His friends kept away from him and called him Yohanan who eats hallot. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi accepted this as proof and declared him a priest.

05.event: On his deathbed Mar Ukva asked for his charity records and saw he had given seven thousand gold dinars.
05.turn: He felt this was too little for the journey to the World-to-Come.
05.outcome: He got up and gave away half of his remaining money to charity.
05.summary: As Mar Ukva was dying he asked for his charity records and found he had given seven thousand gold dinars. He said his provisions were light and the road long. He then gave half of what he still owned to charity, and the Gemara explained why this did not break the one-fifth limit.

06.event: Rabbi Yohanan objected to Rabbi Elazar's claim that the uneducated will not be resurrected, and Rabbi Elazar answered with another verse.
06.turn: Seeing Rabbi Yohanan grieved, Rabbi Elazar said he had found a remedy for the uneducated.
06.outcome: He offered a way for them to share in life: supporting Torah scholars counts as cleaving to God.
06.summary: Rabbi Elazar said the uneducated would not live again. Rabbi Yohanan objected that God would not like that said of ordinary Jews. When Rabbi Elazar saw him distressed, he offered a way out: those who marry their daughters to scholars or support scholars are credited as cleaving to God.
06.missing: It is mostly a scriptural exchange with little event; the ending is a teaching rather than a narrated outcome.

07.actor: Rav, as agent for Rabba bar bar Hana
07.event: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy him a plot of land, and Rav bought it for himself.
07.turn: This seemed deceitful, but the land was in a valley of violent men who respected Rav and not Rabba.
07.outcome: The Gemara justified Rav, who feared someone else would buy the land before he could inform Rabba.
07.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy land for him, but Rav bought it for himself. This looked like deceit. The Gemara explained that the local violent men would sell only to Rav, and that Rav acted at once because someone else might have bought it while he went to inform Rabba.

08.event: Rav Avya came to Neharde'a and saw a man tying a bolt to a door with a reed.
08.outcome: He ruled that the door may not be locked on Shabbat with it.
08.summary: Rav Avya visited Neharde'a and saw a man tying a bolt to his door with a reed. He said that the door could not be locked with it on Shabbat.
08.missing: No turn or consequence is given; it is a brief ruling reported as an incident.

09.actor: Rav Aha bar Abba and his son-in-law Rav Hisda
09.event: Rav Aha visited Rav Hisda and sat his granddaughter on his lap.
09.turn: Rav Hisda asked whether she might already be betrothed, and each accused the other of breaking a ruling of Rav or Shmuel.
09.outcome: Rav Aha answered that Shmuel permits such acts done for the sake of Heaven.
09.summary: Rav Aha visited his son-in-law Rav Hisda and put his granddaughter on his lap. Rav Hisda asked whether she might be betrothed. Rav Aha replied that Rav Hisda broke Rav's ruling by betrothing his daughter as a minor, and Rav Hisda answered that Rav Aha broke Shmuel's ruling about using a woman. Rav Aha said another view of Shmuel permits it when done for the sake of Heaven.

10.event: He had a great deal of movable property he wanted to give as a gift and was told it must be transferred through land.
10.turn: He bought a plot near Jerusalem and declared a part of it, with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels, to go to someone.
10.outcome: He died, and the Sages upheld his statement.
10.summary: A man in Jerusalem wanted to give away much movable property. The Sages told him he had to transfer it with land. He bought a plot and said a part of it, with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels, belonged to a named person. He died and the Sages carried out his words.

11.actor: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
11.event: His sharecropper, who usually brought fruit on Friday, brought it on Thursday because he had a court case before him.
11.turn: Rabbi Yishmael refused the fruit and disqualified himself as judge, then found himself thinking of ways the man could win.
11.outcome: He had other scholars judge the case and cursed those who take bribes, since even he was biased without taking anything.
11.summary: Rabbi Yishmael's sharecropper brought a basket of fruit on a Thursday, not Friday, because he had a case to bring. Rabbi Yishmael refused it and said he could not judge the case. Two scholars judged it, but he kept thinking of ways the man might win, and concluded that those who really take bribes must be even more biased.

12.actor: Rami bar Hama's sister and her husband Rav Avya
12.event: Her marriage contract was lost and the couple came before Rav Yosef.
12.turn: Rav Yosef cited Rabbi Meir's view that they were forbidden to each other, the Rabbis said it was permitted, and Abaye objected that the law follows Rabbi Meir's decrees.
12.outcome: Rav Yosef told Rav Avya to go and write her a new marriage contract.
12.summary: Rami bar Hama's sister was married to Rav Avya, and her marriage contract was lost. They asked Rav Yosef, who cited Rabbi Meir's strict view and the Rabbis' lenient one. Abaye said the law follows Rabbi Meir, so Rav Yosef told Rav Avya to write her a new contract.

13.actor: A man testifying before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
13.event: He said another man had the presumed status of a Levite because he had been called to read second in the synagogue.
13.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua asked if this was due to his being a Levite or to prominence, and the man said a priest had read before him.
13.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi accepted his word and elevated the man to Levite status.
13.summary: A man told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that someone was a Levite because he was called to read second in the synagogue. Rabbi Yehoshua asked if that was because he was a Levite or just prominent. The man said a priest read before him, and Rabbi Yehoshua accepted his word and elevated him to Levite status.

14.event: A man asked Rabbi Yosei whether a widow could perform halitza within three months of her husband's death.
14.turn: Rabbi Yosei said no, and when the man asked what harm there would be, Rabbi Yosei cited a verse.
14.outcome: The verse shows that only someone eligible for levirate marriage may perform halitza.
14.summary: A man asked Rabbi Yosei whether halitza could be done within three months of the husband's death. Rabbi Yosei said it could not. When the man asked what harm it would do, Rabbi Yosei recited a verse from which he derived that anyone eligible for halitza must also be eligible for levirate marriage.
14.missing: It is a question and answer with a legal conclusion rather than a story with events.

15.actor: A man in Shihin whose father left him mustard stalks
15.event: One of three mustard branches left by his father broke, and nine kav of mustard were found on it.
15.outcome: They roofed a craftsmen's booth with its wood.
15.summary: In Shihin a man's father left him three mustard branches. One broke and nine kav of mustard were found on it, and its wood was used to roof a potters' booth. Rabbi Shimon ben Tahlifa added that his father left a cabbage stalk they climbed with a ladder.
15.missing: It is a marvel offered as proof of future abundance, with no real turn.

16.actor: Rav Pappa and Yehuda bar Mareimar
16.event: Rav Pappa went to arrange his son's marriage contract with Abba of Sura, and Yehuda bar Mareimar came to honor him but would not enter the house.
16.turn: Rav Pappa pressed him to enter, and his silent presence led Abba of Sura to write all his property into the dowry.
16.outcome: Yehuda said that even this was not to his liking, so Abba of Sura offered to retract, and Yehuda said he should keep his agreement.
16.summary: Rav Pappa went to write his son's marriage contract, and Yehuda bar Mareimar met him but hesitated at the door. Rav Pappa persuaded him to enter. He sat silent, and Abba of Sura thought he was angry and wrote all his property into the dowry. Yehuda said he did not like even that. Abba offered to retract, and Yehuda said he should not.

17.actor: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda, Marei bar Mar and Rav Huna's son Rabba
17.event: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda sent word asking Rav Huna whether the law follows Rabbi Elazar on bills of divorce.
17.turn: Before the request arrived, Rav Huna died.
17.outcome: His son Rabba answered from his father's tradition that the law follows Rabbi Elazar.
17.summary: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda sent a request to ask Rav Huna whether the law follows Rabbi Elazar on bills of divorce. Rav Huna died before it reached him. His son Rabba said that his father had taught, in Rava's name, that the law follows Rabbi Elazar, and others had the same ruling from Rav.

18.event: Orphan daughters came before Shmuel about movable property held for them by Rabbi Banai.
18.outcome: Shmuel told Rabbi Banai to go and sustain them.
18.summary: Rabbi Banai held movable property that belonged to orphans, and the orphan daughters came before Shmuel. He told Rabbi Banai to go and sustain them.
18.missing: No turn or ending beyond the instruction; it is cited as a proof for a legal question.

19.actor: A divorced woman, Shmuel and Rav Dimi bar Yosef
19.event: A divorcee who did not want to nurse her son came before Shmuel, who sent Rav Dimi to check if the child recognized her.
19.turn: Rav Dimi put her among women and carried the child past them, and the child looked at her joyfully while she looked away.
19.outcome: Rav Dimi told her to lift her eyes and take her son.
19.summary: A divorced woman came before Shmuel, unwilling to nurse her son. Shmuel sent Rav Dimi bar Yosef to see if the child knew her. Rav Dimi put her in a row of women and carried the child past, and the child looked at her gladly while she looked away. He told her to lift her eyes and take her son.

20.event: Ravina held wine belonging to his orphaned nephew and was taking his own wine to Sikhra to sell.
20.turn: He asked Rav Ashi whether he could bring the orphan's wine too.
20.outcome: Rav Ashi told him to go, since the orphan's wine was no better than his own.
20.summary: Ravina held wine belonging to his orphaned nephew, and also had his own wine to take to Sikhra. He asked Rav Ashi if he could take the orphan's wine too. Rav Ashi said yes, because the orphan's wine was no better than his own.
